clue.text: Lead taken to finish the game

definitions.text: Lead taken to finish the game

blocks.note: a buck is a male deer, a classic game animal
lead pellets fired from a gun are shot

explanation.surface: A player or team goes ahead and seals victory in a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' reads as being in front, and 'game' as a contest. 'Taken to finish' puts the lead after the game, and read whole the clue describes ammunition used to kill deer.
explanation.definitionFit: Buckshot is coarse metal shot loaded into shotgun cartridges for killing deer and other large quarry.

clue.text: Two-headed elbow-bender?

blocks.note: surface reading: a two-headed drinker, since bending the elbow means drinking
setter's reading: the upper-arm muscle with two heads that flexes the elbow

explanation.surface: A monstrous drinker with two heads.
explanation.walkthrough: To bend the elbow is slang for drinking alcohol; literally, the muscle that bends the elbow has two points of origin.
explanation.definitionFit: The muscle at the front of the upper arm has two heads of origin and flexes the forearm at the joint.

clue.text: Corporation in vote against City's disgraceful behaviour

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the joined pair that follows

blocks.note: a con is a vote against, as in pros and cons
corporation is old slang for a pot belly, and a tum is a belly
Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire

explanation.surface: A council ballot against a city's outrageous conduct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' reads as a town council; it is old slang for a paunch. Ely is a small cathedral city in the English fens.
explanation.definitionFit: Contumely is insolent, scornful treatment or insulting language, behaviour that brings shame on the person showing it.

clue.text: Result, incidentally, of bowling having deteriorated

blocks.note: spin is a style of bowling in cricket
food that has gone bad is off

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator's aside on what happened when the bowling got worse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Incidentally' looks like a conversational aside but belongs to the definition: a by-product.
explanation.definitionFit: A spin-off is a secondary benefit or product arising incidentally from some larger project or activity.

clue.text: Unfertilized seed of universal love, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters are only one possible arrangement, so they are reordered

blocks.note: U is the film certificate for universal viewing
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sentimental phrase about the seed of a love shared by all.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the British film rating for universal; it joins the letters of love to be reordered.
explanation.definitionFit: In botany an ovule is the structure in a plant ovary that becomes a seed once fertilized.

clue.text: Backward schoolkid's howler

indicators.note: a backward child is slow, but backward here means the word is read from its end to its start

blocks.note: schoolkids are pupils; the 's makes it plural

explanation.surface: A slow child at school makes a howling mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backward' pretends to describe the child's ability. A howler is a glaring blunder, often a schoolboy one.
explanation.definitionFit: A howler is an embarrassing blunder, and a slip-up is likewise an obvious careless error or mistake.

clue.text: Gander appears to need double energy

blocks.note: looks means seems or appears
E is the symbol for energy, doubled

explanation.surface: A male goose seems to require twice the energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gander' looks like the male goose, but 'take a gander' is slang for a quick look.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal words for a quick glance or inspection at something, as in having a peek.

clue.text: This priest digs soldiers

blocks.note: digs and pad are both slang for lodgings
RE is the Royal Engineers, a regiment of soldiers

explanation.surface: A clergyman who is keen on troops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digs' reads as a verb, slang for likes; it is the noun for lodgings, as is PAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Padre is the usual name for a military chaplain, a priest who serves with the armed forces.

clue.text: Where unusually happy individual can make his money talk

definitions.text: Where unusually happy individual can make his money talk

indicators.note: unusually means not in the normal way, so the letters take an unusual order

blocks.note: taken as written
an individual is one person

explanation.surface: A cheerful person spends cash to do the talking.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: coins put in one let a caller talk, so his money makes speech possible.
explanation.definitionFit: A coin-operated public telephone takes cash to let someone make a call, so the money buys conversation.

clue.text: Refractory remnant delivered

blocks.note: a stub is the short part left over, as of a pencil or ticket
a baby that has been delivered is born

explanation.surface: A leftover piece of heat-resistant material has been handed over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refractory' can mean heat-resistant, as in brick, but here it is the older sense of obstinate.
explanation.definitionFit: A refractory person resists control or discipline, which is to be obstinate and unyielding.

clue.text: No time to stop in the Stock Exchange

definitions.text: No time to stop in the Stock Exchange

blocks.clueFragment: No time to stop in the Stock Exchange
blocks.note: surface reading: a trader is too busy to linger on the trading floor

blocks.clueFragment: No time to stop in the Stock Exchange
blocks.note: setter's reading: the settlement day on which a bargain is carried over rather than closed

explanation.surface: Busy dealers on the trading floor have no chance for a break.
explanation.walkthrough: On the old London Stock Exchange, the day on which bargains could be carried forward to the next account, instead of being settled, was the day for carrying on, not stopping.
explanation.definitionFit: On the old London exchange this was the first settlement day, when deals were rolled forward into the next trading account instead of being closed.

clue.text: Chimney fitted into baffle that is feathered

indicators.note: something fitted into a space sits inside it, so one word goes within the other

blocks.note: to pose someone is to puzzle or baffle them, as with a hard question
lum is a Scottish and northern word for a chimney

explanation.surface: A chimney is fitted with a baffle plate that has a feathered edge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Baffle' looks like a noun for a chimney part, but it is a verb meaning puzzle, as when a question poses a problem.
explanation.definitionFit: Plumose is a botanical and zoological term for something bearing plumes or feather-like branches, so feathery in form.

clue.text: Sue provides a bachelor with cheese-spread

indicators.note: spread suggests something smeared about and out of shape, so the letters are scattered into a new order

blocks.note: B is the standard abbreviation for bachelor, as in degrees
the six letters of the word, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone named Sue serves a single man a cheese spread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sue' looks like a woman's name but is a verb meaning plead. 'Cheese-spread' looks like a food; only 'cheese' is the material, rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To sue can mean to entreat or petition someone, which is what it is to beseech them earnestly.

clue.text: This cigar produces a superb ring!

blocks.note: superb and flawless are near synonyms
a ring is round, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: An exclamation of delight at the fine band around a cigar.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'ring' sounds like a cigar band or smoke ring; it is just the round letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A perfecto is a type of cigar, thick in the middle and tapering to a point at both ends.

clue.text: Ready with simple sweater?

definitions.note: the wool stands for a garment made of it

blocks.note: the ready is slang for ready money, cash
mere means simple, nothing more than

explanation.surface: Is a plain jumper all set to wear?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' reads as prepared; it is the noun, British slang for money on hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A knitted jumper made of the fine soft wool from Kashmir goats is often simply called by that fibre's name.

clue.text: Low-flying leaders going through a Gothic arch

indicators.note: leaders are those at the front, so only the opening letter of each word is kept
to go through something is to pass inside it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: Gothic here means German, and the German for a is ein
the opening letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Aircraft flying low pass through the pointed arch of a Gothic cathedral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gothic arch' reads as a piece of church architecture, but Gothic points to German, and 'arch' is the adjective meaning roguish.
explanation.definitionFit: An arch look is playfully mischievous, and elfin likewise describes a small, impish, mischievous charm.

clue.text: Parry brings everybody to the greenwood

blocks.note: the greenwood is a wood in leaf, as in Robin Hood's forest
everybody is all of them

explanation.surface: Someone named Parry leads a crowd into the woods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parry' reads like a surname, but it is the verb to ward off a blow. 'Brings everybody to' places the second piece after the first.
explanation.definitionFit: To parry a blow is to ward it off in advance, and to forestall is to prevent something by acting first.

clue.text: Musical baggage-handler?

blocks.note: first meaning: the Rodgers and Hammerstein stage show
second meaning: the rotating belt that brings luggage to airport passengers

explanation.surface: A porter who likes to sing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Musical' reads as an adjective describing the handler; it is a noun, the 1945 show set around a fairground ride.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a 1945 Broadway show and the revolving conveyor from which airport travellers collect their suitcases.

clue.text: Gorge some of baby's sweets

indicators.note: some of means only a part, so the letters lie within the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the words, after the first b

explanation.surface: Someone stuffs themselves with a share of an infant's sweets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gorge' reads as a verb meaning eat greedily; it is the noun, a deep ravine.
explanation.definitionFit: A gorge is a deep narrow ravine, and an abyss is a similarly deep chasm or bottomless pit.

clue.text: Jabber in the clinic

blocks.note: surface reading: someone chattering away in a doctor's waiting room
setter's reading: the thing that gives patients a jab, an injection

explanation.surface: Someone babbling away at the doctor's surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jabber' reads as a chatterer; split as jab-ber it is whatever does the jabbing.
explanation.definitionFit: A hypodermic is the instrument with a needle and plunger used to inject patients, giving them a jab.

clue.text: Cruise casually around north-east in comfortable berth

indicators.note: casually means carelessly and without order, so the letters are thrown into a new arrangement
around means encircling, so one set of letters wraps the other

blocks.note: the six letters of the word, to be rearranged
NE is the compass abbreviation for north-east

explanation.surface: Taking a relaxed sea voyage towards the north-east in a cosy ship's cabin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Berth' and 'cruise' suggest a ship, but a comfortable berth is also an easy post or job.
explanation.definitionFit: A cushy berth is an easy job, and a sinecure is a paid office requiring little or no actual work.

clue.text: Fiery torch taken up by Pole

definitions.text: Fiery torch taken up by Pole

blocks.clueFragment: Fiery torch taken up by Pole
blocks.note: surface reading: a Polish person lifts a blazing flame, like a torch-bearer

blocks.clueFragment: Fiery torch taken up by Pole
blocks.note: setter's reading: a metal basket of burning fuel mounted high on a staff

explanation.surface: A Polish athlete raises the flaming torch.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital P makes 'Pole' look like a person from Poland; it is a wooden staff, on which this beacon is carried aloft.
explanation.definitionFit: A cresset is an iron basket or cup holding burning oil or pitch, carried on a staff as a beacon.

clue.text: Wheat's cut down with a sweep of the scythe

indicators.note: a crop cut down is knocked flat and jumbled, so the letters fall into a new order

blocks.note: all six letters, including the s, taken for rearranging

explanation.surface: A field of grain is mown with the long curved blade of a scythe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut down' looks like part of the harvest picture, and the definition does too; only the possessive word supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A swathe is the strip of grass or grain cut by a single stroke of a scythe, or the width covered.

clue.text: Crude tattoo beaten by the West Indians

definitions.text: Crude tattoo beaten by the West Indians

blocks.note: crude is unrefined petroleum
a tattoo is a drumbeat, and to drum is to tattoo

explanation.surface: A rough rhythm played by Caribbean musicians.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue describes the steel pans of Trinidad, beaten out of old containers once used to hold crude.
explanation.definitionFit: Caribbean steel pans were first made from discarded steel barrels that had held petroleum, so these barrels are the instruments beaten there.

clue.text: Slow movement of longship

blocks.note: the one printed word is read split in two, as long followed by ship
L is an abbreviation for long, as in long. for longitude
the Argo was the ship of Jason and the Argonauts

explanation.surface: A Viking vessel moving sluggishly through the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Longship' reads as one Viking vessel; split, it is L plus Jason's ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Largo is the musical tempo marking for a very slow, broad pace, and so names a slow movement in a symphony.

clue.text: There's a cutting edge to this maxim on the decorative border

definitions.text: There's a cutting edge to this

blocks.note: a fret is an ornamental pattern of interlaced lines used as a border
a saw is an old saying or maxim

explanation.surface: A pointed proverb printed along an ornamental edging.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue, X on Y puts X after Y. 'Cutting edge' sounds like a sharp remark but is literal: the tool has teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: A fretsaw is a fine-bladed saw for cutting curved patterns in wood, so it literally has a cutting edge.

clue.text: Sofa's disposed of in the Depression

indicators.note: disposed means arranged or set out, so the letters are put into a fresh order

blocks.note: all five letters, including the s, taken for rearranging

explanation.surface: A settee is thrown out during a period of gloom or economic slump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disposed of' reads as thrown away; 'disposed' alone means arranged. 'Depression' is a hollow, not gloom.
explanation.definitionFit: In anatomy a fossa is a shallow hollow or pit in a bone or other surface, a physical dip.

clue.text: Keeping, in good shape, unaffected by psychiatrist

blocks.note: first meaning: of fabric that keeps its size when washed
second meaning, read literally: able to hold out against a shrink, slang for a psychiatrist

explanation.surface: Someone stays fit and well without any help from therapy.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half takes the compound word literally; shrink is slang for a psychiatrist, short for headshrinker.
explanation.definitionFit: Treated cloth that does not contract in the wash holds its original size and form after laundering.

clue.text: Nobody, given fresh start, is a pillager

indicators.note: a fresh start means the opening letter is swapped for a new one

blocks.note: Charles Pooter is the hero of the comic novel The Diary of a Nobody

explanation.surface: An unknown person, given a second chance in life, turns to plundering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nobody' reads as no person; it is Mr Pooter of the Grossmiths' 1892 novel The Diary of a Nobody. His P is replaced by L.
explanation.definitionFit: A pillager plunders goods by force, and one who loots is exactly that kind of plunderer or thief.

clue.text: Spill tea, upset when it is sweet

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the eight letters taken together for rearranging

explanation.surface: Someone is cross at spilling a cup of tea, though it was sugared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spill' and 'upset' both seem to describe the accident; only 'upset' does the work.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastille is a small flavoured lozenge or sweet, often fruit-flavoured or medicated, sucked slowly.
